extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and advanced students working on numerical algebraic methods, geometric constructions, and problem-solvers reading a 19th-century mathematical journal
extracted.subtask_description: Techniques and heuristics for synthesizing/analyzing numerical roots of polynomials (Horner-type methods), with worked examples and geometric-construction solutions; includes practical rules for arranging multiplications and contractions to minimize error and simplify work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose digit-order to suit the operation
rubrics_metrics.description: The order in which the digits of the root are taken is optional; one may commence with the final digit (least significant) or with the first digit (most significant), according to convenience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two varieties are illustrated: starting with final digit (use multipliers a p times then diminish from right) and commencing with first digit (founded on coefficients of (2°+8)’, usual cube-root method). Choose the ordering that best stabilizes divisors and coefficients for the intended analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commence with leading digits to increase stability
rubrics_metrics.description: By commencing at the top of the numerical scale (leading digits) we ensure increasing stability of the divisor and coefficients in general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach is best adapted to analysis because it produces a tolerably trustworthy divisor in the first instance; the text recommends this ordering for general convenience of the reader and for analytic purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer methods that minimize addends and mixed mental operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use methods that employ fewer addends and determine them by multiplication alone, avoiding the combined mental use of multiplication and addition where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'new method' described transforms by radical digits alone and thereby reduces opportunities for slips; 'moulded precision' in alternative methods reduces error but the new method's fewer addends is an important advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin multiplications with the left-hand figure of the multiplier
rubrics_metrics.description: In multiplying, begin with the left-hand figure of the multiplier to facilitate the formation of additions and later contraction of inferior addends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Starting at the left simplifies alignment of partial products and makes it easier to manage carried products as they advance one place further to the right for successive products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule for positioning the first addend (p, m rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the new coefficient in any column advances p figures to the right of the old one and is to be multiplied by m digits, the first addend to the next old coefficient must begin p + 1 − (m − 1) places to the right of it (i.e., p − m + 2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If p ≥ 2 this may imply starting to the left; making p negative gives the analogous rule for commencing contractions (cutting off digits). This rule governs alignment of addends when multiplying or contracting in the tabular transformations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graphical layout: mark first addend with vertical lines and cut others with points
rubrics_metrics.description: Designate the extent of the first addend by vertical lines; the remaining m − 1 places of each new coefficient may be cut off singly by points and partially neglected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At each subsequent contraction, draw the vertical line at a uniform interval left of the points. This visual discipline helps keep contracted multiplication organized and avoids misalignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use known special cases to determine constants
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine undetermined constants in functional or trial expressions by substituting particular known cases (e.g., three specially chosen values) and solving the resulting system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by taking three particular angles/values to fix constants C and C' in assumed functional forms; this is a standard technique for fitting parameters to satisfy a functional equation and boundary cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject solutions that make coefficients or constants infinite or impossible
rubrics_metrics.description: If a candidate solution causes constants to become infinite or yields impossible values (e.g., impossible roots of unity), reject that solution as extraneous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: if substitution would make C' infinite, or e^3 equals an impossible cube root of −1 yielding contradictions, these roots are rejected. Always test for and exclude such pathological cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check domain constraints and eliminate extraneous roots
rubrics_metrics.description: Verify that candidate roots satisfy the domain constraints (e.g., nonzero denominators, sine/cosine values within allowable ranges) and eliminate those that violate constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: if sin α = 0 leads to infinite constants it must be rejected; prefer solutions satisfying trigonometric domain restrictions and any other implicit assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use depressed equations after finding one root, but beware numerical complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a root is determined accurately, the absolute term is effectively cancelled and a depressed polynomial can be formed to find remaining roots; theoretically depression and continuous approximation coincide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although depressed formulas are fit for solution (especially with pure transformées), practical inconveniences (many digits in residual coefficients and complex contractions) may make evolving each root separately preferable in computation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer pure transformée method for algebraic neatness when feasible
rubrics_metrics.description: The method of pure transformées yields a depressed formula that is a pure function of the remaining roots, each diminished by the known root, and often is algebraically neat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method gives 'moulded precision' and reduces chances of arrangement slips, but weigh this against practical digit-handling costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit trivial preliminary lines in practical calculation
rubrics_metrics.description: In ordinary calculation, initial preparatory lines or valuations that are only illustrative may be dispensed with to economize work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The example of cube of 835271 shows the first two illustrative lines could have been omitted; include such details only when they aid understanding or pedagogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: When solving geometry/construction problems, choose coordinates/planes to simplify
rubrics_metrics.description: Select axes or projection planes (e.g., take one given line as axis or choose plane through AB parallel to CD) to simplify equations and make true lengths/projections immediate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In 3D construction problems use descriptive-geometry projections or choose ground/vertical planes so that required distances and true inclinations are readily obtainable; reduces algebraic/computational effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use projections and revolutions in descriptive geometry to find spatial constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply projections (horizontal and vertical) and, where helpful, imagine revolutions of planar figures about axes to determine positions and true lengths of auxiliary points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: to find a point K perpendicular to a plane, revolve triangle EHF to bring it into a projection plane and use perpendiculars to derive K's projections; this simplifies 3D reasoning by 2D constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impose equal-root/tangency conditions via discriminant or equal-roots criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: When deriving a curve tangent to lines (e.g., parabola escribed to triangle), impose the condition for equal roots (double root) to enforce tangency and solve for parameters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set variable = 0 and require equal roots; eliminate auxiliary parameters (like m) between resulting relations to obtain necessary parameter conditions. Use this to derive tangency constraints or parameter relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check sign and ordering constraints when deducing parameter inequalities
rubrics_metrics.description: When deducing parameter relations from algebraic conditions, verify implied inequalities (e.g., c > b) required for the geometric configuration or algebraic assumptions to hold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the escribed parabola example, deducing that c > b is necessary for the parabola to be escribed as supposed. Always track which inequalities are implied and required for validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce algebraic problems to standard forms (determinants, symmetric forms) for conic and line relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Write conic or line systems in canonical symmetric forms (e.g., quadratic form with coefficients, or linear coefficients normalized) to facilitate elimination and recognition of conditions (e.g., six points on a conic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: represent lines as aa+by−1=0 and conic as quadratic form, determine P,Q by matching coefficients, and exploit determinant relations; this organizes elimination and identification of shared conics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use elimination stepwise and exploit linear dependencies to reduce independent conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: When solving for parameters from multiple constraints, eliminate variables step-by-step and recognize when one condition is a consequence of others, reducing to the minimal independent set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In showing two triangles have a circumscribing conic, three coefficient conditions reduce to two independent ones; exploit such dependencies to simplify solving for unknowns.
